report.source_text: As per our local guidelines and the paediatric neurology consultation, this patient disability grade was static (2–3) and did not worsen during admission. Conversely, he Clinically improved gradually during hospital stay, hence intravenous immunoglobulin was not given.17 He was managed conservatively, monitoring active symptoms as well as peak flow to ensure no respiratory involvement. His peak flows remained normal throughout admission (ranging from 210 to 240). He had ongoing back and leg pain, for which he was successfully treated for using analgesics along with an increasing dose of gabapentin 10 mg/kg once a day on day 1, 10 mg/ kg two times per day a day on day 2, 10 mg/kg three times per day on day 3 and then stopped. He obtained regular physiotherapy in order to regain skills and to avoid any muscle wasting.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 9-year-old boy presented with worsening back pain, unsteadiness, and lower limb weakness. Neurological examination revealed lower limb areflexia. CSF analysis showed albuminocytological dissociation, and MRI demonstrated enhancement of facial nerves and cauda equina. A plain spine X-ray was normal. The patient's disability grade remained static, and he gradually improved with conservative management and physiotherapy, without requiring intravenous immunoglobulin.
